subtopics.title: Key Facts & Formulas
subtopics.subtitle: Formulas, classification tables and VHDL rules from every section of the chapter

concepts.text: Computer organization and embedded-system questions come from a compact set of formulas (pipeline speedup, cache access time, memory sizes, schedulability bounds), a few classification tables (Flynn, cache mapping, RTOS scheduling, IC technologies) and VHDL syntax. This page gathers them section by section; the subtopics carry the derivations and worked examples.

concepts.text: Addressing modes and their effective address:
items: Immediate: operand is in the instruction. Register: operand in a register. Register indirect: EA = R.
Direct: EA = address field. Indirect: EA = M[address field]. Relative: EA = PC + offset.
Indexed: EA = XR + address. Base-register: EA = BR + address. Autoincrement/decrement: EA = R, then R ± 1.

items: Structural: two stages need the same resource → duplicate units or stall.
Data (RAW, WAR, WAW): an instruction needs a result not yet written → forwarding/bypassing, stalls, reordering.
Control: branches change the PC → delayed branch, branch prediction, flushing.

any line; needs comparators on every line

items: Replacement: LRU (best hit rate), FIFO, LFU, random. Write policy: write-through (memory always current, more traffic) vs write-back (dirty bit, fewer writes).
Levels: L1 (split I/D, fastest), L2, L3 (shared). Larger line size exploits spatial locality up to a point.
Locality: temporal (reuse soon) and spatial (neighbours next).

concepts.text: DMA sequence: DREQ → CPU asserts HLDA (bus grant) → DMAC drives address/count → transfer (burst, cycle stealing or transparent) → word count reaches zero → interrupt CPU.
items: Burst: whole block, CPU idle. Cycle stealing: one word per grabbed bus cycle. Transparent: only when the CPU is not using the bus.

items: Critical section protected by a semaphore or by an indivisible test-and-set instruction (spin lock).
Interprocessor arbitration: serial (daisy chain), parallel (priority encoder), dynamic (time slice, polling, LRU, FIFO, rotating daisy chain).
Cache coherence: write-invalidate (snoopy) or directory protocols.

concepts.text: Design metrics: NRE cost, unit cost, size, performance, power, flexibility, time-to-prototype, time-to-market, maintainability, correctness, safety — improving one usually worsens another.
items: Custom single-purpose processor = datapath (registers, functional units, muxes) + controller (FSM); designed from a program via an FSMD.
Optimize the program, then the FSMD (merge/split states), the datapath (share units), and the FSM (state encoding, minimization).

concepts.plainText: Rate-monotonic schedulability: utilisation ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1) (0.693 as n grows); EDF: utilisation ≤ 1

items: Ready → Running → Blocked (waiting) → Ready; context switch saves the task's registers and stack pointer.
Binary semaphore / mutex for mutual exclusion, counting semaphore for resources, queues and mailboxes for messages, event flags for signalling.
Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption and circular wait.

concepts.text: Revision questions often combine two ideas: a pipeline with stalls, a cache address split with an access time, or a disk feeding a DMA controller. The drills below give one worked line per formula, so that each substitution can be checked in seconds. Before substituting, write down the assumptions the answer depends on: KB = 1024 or 1000 bytes, byte- or word-addressable memory, hierarchical or simultaneous cache access, and whether the pipeline stalls. Most wrong options in numeric questions come from dropping exactly one of these.

CPU and pipeline drill
Pipeline k = 6, tp = 2 ns, n = 60 tasks, no stalls:
  T = (k + n - 1) tp = 65 x 2 = 130 ns; unpipelined n k tp = 720 ns
  S = 720 / 130 = 5.54; efficiency = S / k = 0.92; S -> 6 for large n
  with 8 stall cycles: T = (65 + 8) x 2 = 146 ns
CPU time: IC = 2 x 10^6, CPI = 1.5, f = 500 MHz
  T = IC x CPI / f = 3 x 10^6 / (5 x 10^8) = 6 ms; MIPS = 500 / 1.5 = 333
Effective CPI = ideal CPI + stall cycles per instruction:
  15% branches x 3 stall cycles -> CPI = 1 + 0.15 x 3 = 1.45
Amdahl, f = 0.9 on N = 8: S = 1 / (0.1 + 0.9/8) = 4.71 (limit 1/0.1 = 10)

concepts.plainText: CPU time = instruction count × CPI ÷ clock rate; MIPS = clock rate ÷ (CPI × 10^6)

concepts.text:
Memory drill (KB = 1024 bytes, 32-bit byte addresses)
Cache 64 KB, 32-byte lines: lines = 65536 / 32 = 2048, offset = 5 bits
  direct: line 11, tag 32 - 11 - 5 = 16
  4-way:  512 sets -> set 9, tag 18;  fully associative: tag 27
EAT with tc = 2 ns, tm = 50 ns, h = 0.95:
  simultaneous: 0.95 x 2 + 0.05 x 50 = 4.4 ns
  hierarchical: 2 + 0.05 x 50 = 4.5 ns (a miss pays tc + tm)
Composition: 64K x 8 from 16K x 4 chips
  (64K / 16K) x (8 / 4) = 4 rows x 2 chips = 8 chips
  16 address lines: A13-A0 to every chip, A15-A14 to a 2-to-4 decoder

concepts.plainText: Disk access time = average seek + half a revolution + transfer of b bytes (r revolutions per second, N bytes per track)

concepts.text:
Arithmetic and I/O drill
Booth, multiplier 0111 1000 (+120): pairs (Qi, Qi-1) differ at bits 3 and 7
  subtract M at bit 3, add M at bit 7 -> 2 operations; 120 = 2^7 - 2^3
IEEE 754 single: -6.75 = -110.11b = -1.1011 x 2^2
  s = 1, e = 2 + 127 = 129 = 1000 0001, f = 1011 0...0 -> C0D8 0000H
Disk: Ts = 4 ms, 7200 rpm (r = 120 rev/s), 500 sectors/track, 1 sector
  Ta = 4 ms + 1/240 s + 1/(120 x 500) s = 4 + 4.167 + 0.017 = 8.18 ms
DMA cycle stealing: 4 MB/s (1 MB = 10^6 B), 32-bit words -> 10^6 words/s
  60 ns per stolen cycle -> 10^6 x 60 ns = 6% of memory cycles
DMA burst: 4 KB (1 KB = 1024 B) on a 32-bit bus, 50 ns per bus cycle
  -> 1024 words x 50 ns = 51.2 µs

RTOS, control and embedded drill
RM bound n(2^(1/n) - 1): n = 2 -> 0.828, 3 -> 0.780, 4 -> 0.757, n -> inf: 0.693
  (C,T) = (1,4), (2,8), (1,10): U = 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.10 = 0.60 <= 0.780 -> RM safe
  (C,T) = (1,4), (2,5), (2,6):  U = 0.25 + 0.40 + 0.33 = 0.98 > 0.780
    bound inconclusive; response time of (2,6): R = 2 + 2x1 + 2x2 = 8 > 6
    -> RM misses, while EDF meets every deadline because U <= 1
Closed loop: G = 200, H = 0.045 -> GH = 9, Y/R = 200 / 10 = 20 (1/H = 22.2)
  G falls 10% to 180: 180 / 9.1 = 19.78, only 1.1% lower
NRE break-even: A = $15k + $30/unit, B = $90k + $5/unit
  N = (90k - 15k) / (30 - 5) = 3000 units; above 3000, B is cheaper
Watchdog: 32.768 kHz / 128 = 256 Hz tick; 1024 counts -> 4 s timeout

rows: SISD: one uniprocessor, even when pipelined; SIMD: array, vector and GPU lanes; MISD: practically unused; MIMD: multicores, multiprocessors, clusters
RISC: fixed length, load/store, many registers, hardwired, CPI near 1. CISC: variable length, memory operands, many modes, microprogrammed
Write-through (usually with no-write-allocate): memory always current. Write-back (usually with write-allocate): dirty bit, memory written on eviction
Compulsory (first reference), capacity (cache too small), conflict (mapping); more associativity removes only conflict misses
bit, boolean, integer, real, character, time in STANDARD; std_logic (resolved, 9 values) in std_logic_1164; signed and unsigned in numeric_std
'U' uninitialised, 'X' unknown, '0', '1', 'Z' high impedance, 'W' weak unknown, 'L' weak 0, 'H' weak 1, '-' don't care
Usable space (n disks of size D)
Bit- or byte-interleaved striping, dedicated parity disk
Block striping, parity rotated over all disks
Two independent parity blocks per stripe
1 (more only if each hits a different pair)
No: dirty, written back on eviction or snoop
No, so a write moves it to M without a bus transaction
Yes, so a write must invalidate the other copies first

concepts.text: Common slips in combined questions: KiB (1024) versus kB (1000) and bits versus bytes; word versus byte addressing when sizing MAR or a tag; counting the cache hit time twice, or not at all, in EAT; forgetting the k − 1 fill cycles or the stall cycles of a pipeline; using the RM bound for the wrong n (0.780 holds only for three tasks); and reading a utilisation above the RM bound as proof of failure, when it only means the test is inconclusive.

formulas.plainText: Pipeline speedup for k stages and n tasks

notes.text: Numeric MCQs in this chapter are almost always one of: pipeline speedup nk/(k + n − 1), cache average access time, address-bit splits (word, line/set, tag), number of chips to compose a memory, or an RMS utilisation check. Write the formula before substituting.

Do not confuse DMA (a hardware controller moves data while the CPU is off the bus) with interrupt-driven I/O (the CPU still moves every word); and do not confuse write-through (memory always updated) with write-back (memory updated only when a dirty line is evicted).

Pairs that get swapped: SIMD (one instruction, many data — GPUs) vs MIMD (multiprocessors); RISC (fixed length, load/store, hardwired) vs CISC (variable length, microprogrammed); signal (scheduled) vs variable (immediate) in VHDL; hard real-time (missed deadline = failure) vs soft real-time (degraded quality).

formulas.title: Pipeline speedup
formulas.description: k stages, n tasks; equal stage times assumed; tends to k for large n.

formulas.title: Cache average access time
formulas.description: h is the hit ratio, t_c the cache time, t_m the main-memory time (add t_c if the miss also pays the cache lookup).

formulas.title: Amdahl's law
formulas.description: f is the parallelisable fraction, N the number of processors; the serial part caps the speedup.

formulas.title: Rate-monotonic bound
formulas.description: C_i execution time, T_i period; sufficient condition, tending to 0.693 for many tasks; EDF allows U ≤ 1.

formulas.title: Closed-loop transfer function
formulas.description: G forward-path gain, H feedback gain; negative feedback reduces the gain but improves accuracy and stability.

flashcards.front: Give the speedup of a 5-stage pipeline processing 20 instructions and its limiting value.
flashcards.back: S = 20 × 5 / (5 + 20 − 1) = 100/24 ≈ 4.17; the limit for many instructions is 5 (the number of stages).

flashcards.front: Name the three cache mapping functions and the address fields each uses.
flashcards.back: Direct (tag, line, word), fully associative (tag, word), set-associative (tag, set, word).

flashcards.front: In VHDL, what is the difference between a signal and a variable assignment?
flashcards.back: signal <= is scheduled and takes effect at the end of the process (or after a delay); variable := is immediate and only exists inside a process/subprogram.

questions.questionText: A 4-stage pipeline executes 12 instructions with a 10 ns stage time. Compared with a non-pipelined unit taking 40 ns per instruction, the speedup is approximately:
questions.explanation: Pipelined time = (4 + 12 − 1) × 10 ns = 150 ns; non-pipelined = 12 × 40 = 480 ns; speedup = 480/150 = 3.2, below the ideal 4.

questions.questionText: A cache has a hit ratio of 0.9, a cache access time of 10 ns and a main-memory access time of 100 ns. The average memory access time is:
How many 2K × 8 memory chips are needed to build an 8K × 16 memory, and how many address lines does the complete memory use?
questions.explanation: 8K/2K = 4 chips per bank for words × 16/8 = 2 chips for width → 8 chips; 8K words need log₂(8192) = 13 address lines (11 to each chip, 2 to a decoder).

questions.questionText: Three periodic tasks have (C, T) = (1, 4), (1, 5) and (1, 10) ms. Under rate-monotonic scheduling they are:
options: Schedulable, since U = 0.55 is below the 3-task bound 0.78
questions.explanation: U = 1/4 + 1/5 + 1/10 = 0.55; the RMS bound for n = 3 is 3(2^(1/3) − 1) ≈ 0.78, so the set is guaranteed schedulable.

questions.questionText: In VHDL, a process whose sensitivity list contains only clk and whose body assigns q <= d inside if rising_edge(clk) describes a:
questions.explanation: Assignment only on the rising clock edge infers an edge-triggered D flip-flop; a latch would come from a level-sensitive incomplete if without a clock edge.

questions.questionText: An 8-stage instruction pipeline with a 2 ns clock runs a program of 60 instructions. Ten of them are branches (the last instruction is not one of them), and each branch stalls the pipeline for 3 clock cycles; there are no other stalls. How long does the program take from the first fetch to the completion of the last instruction?
questions.explanation: Cycles = (k + n − 1) + stalls = (8 + 60 − 1) + 10 × 3 = 67 + 30 = 97, so T = 97 × 2 ns = 194 ns. Forgetting the k − 1 = 7 fill cycles gives 180 ns, ignoring the stalls gives 134 ns, and 960 ns is the non-pipelined time 60 × 8 × 2 ns.

questions.questionText: Eight 2 TB disks are configured either as RAID 10 (four mirrored pairs, striped) or as RAID 6. What usable capacity does each give, and how many disk failures is each guaranteed to survive, whichever disks fail?
options: RAID 10: 8 TB, any 4 failures; RAID 6: 12 TB, any 2 failures
RAID 10: 14 TB, any 1 failure; RAID 6: 12 TB, any 2 failures
RAID 10: 8 TB, any 1 failure; RAID 6: 14 TB, any 1 failure
RAID 10: 8 TB, any 1 failure; RAID 6: 12 TB, any 2 failures
questions.explanation: RAID 10 stores every block twice, so it offers 8 × 2 TB / 2 = 8 TB; it survives four failures only if each hits a different pair, and losing both disks of one pair loses data, so only one failure is guaranteed. RAID 6 keeps two independent parity blocks per stripe: (8 − 2) × 2 TB = 12 TB, surviving any two failures.

questions.questionText: In the nine-valued type std_ulogic of ieee.std_logic_1164, what do the values 'W', 'L' and 'H' stand for?
options: Write enable, logic low and high impedance
questions.explanation: 'W', 'L' and 'H' are the weak (resistive) forms of 'X', '0' and '1', used to model pull-downs and pull-ups; any strong driver overrides them during resolution. High impedance is 'Z', and strong 0 and 1 are '0' and '1'.

questions.questionText: Ten independent periodic tasks, with deadlines equal to their periods, have a total utilisation of 0.72 on one processor. Which conclusion about pre-emptive RM and EDF scheduling follows from the utilisation tests alone?
options: RM is guaranteed, because 0.72 is below the three-task bound of 0.780; EDF is also guaranteed
RM will miss deadlines, because 0.72 exceeds ln 2 ≈ 0.693; only EDF can schedule the set
The RM test is inconclusive, because 0.72 exceeds the ten-task bound of about 0.718; EDF is guaranteed, because U ≤ 1
Neither policy is guaranteed, because no task set with a utilisation above 0.693 can be scheduled
questions.explanation: For n = 10 the Liu and Layland bound is 10(2^(1/10) − 1) ≈ 0.718, and U = 0.72 is just above it, so the sufficient RM test gives no guarantee (the set may still pass response-time analysis). EDF is optimal on one processor and needs only U ≤ 1.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit register holds 1001 1100. What value does it represent as an unsigned number, in sign-magnitude, in 1's complement and in 2's complement, in that order?
questions.explanation: Unsigned: 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 = 156; sign-magnitude: sign 1 with magnitude 001 1100 = 28, so −28. 1's complement: inverting gives 0110 0011 = 99, so −99. 2's complement: 156 − 256 = −100.

questions.questionText: Which pairing of Flynn class and machine is NOT correct?
options: MISD — a multicore desktop processor running several independent programs
SIMD — an array processor whose control unit broadcasts each instruction to many processing elements
MIMD — a shared-memory multiprocessor whose cores run their own instruction streams
questions.explanation: Independent programs on several cores are multiple instruction streams working on multiple data streams, which is MIMD; MISD (many instruction streams on one data stream) has practically no commercial examples. The other three are the textbook pairings, and a pipelined uniprocessor is still SISD.

questions.questionText: A disk spins at 6000 rpm and each track holds 50,000 bytes. Whole tracks are read into memory by a cycle-stealing DMA controller that moves one 32-bit word per stolen memory cycle, and each memory cycle lasts 80 ns. What fraction of all memory cycles does the DMA steal while a track is being read? (1 MB = 10^6 bytes)
questions.explanation: Data rate = 50,000 bytes × (6000 / 60) rev/s = 5 MB/s = 1.25 × 10^6 words/s; stolen fraction = 1.25 × 10^6 × 80 ns = 0.10, i.e. 10%. Moving one byte per cycle gives 40% and 16-bit words give 20%.

questions.questionText: A direct-mapped cache has 1024 lines of 16 bytes, and the byte-addressable main memory is 1 MB (1 MB = 2^20 bytes). How many tag bits does each line store, and how many different memory blocks map to each line?
questions.explanation: The 20-bit address splits into offset 4 (16-byte lines), line 10 (1024 lines) and tag 20 − 10 − 4 = 6. Memory has 2^20 / 16 = 65,536 blocks for 1024 lines, so 64 = 2^6 blocks compete for each line, one per tag value. A 16-bit tag belongs to a fully associative cache.

questions.questionText: An FPGA version of a product needs $20,000 NRE and costs $35 per unit; an ASIC version needs $170,000 NRE and costs $10 per unit. At what production volume do their total costs break even, and what is the per-product cost (total cost ÷ units) at that volume?
questions.explanation: 20,000 + 35N = 170,000 + 10N gives N = 150,000 / 25 = 6,000 units. The total there is 20,000 + 35 × 6,000 = $230,000 (and 170,000 + 10 × 6,000 for the ASIC), so the per-product cost is 230,000 / 6,000 ≈ $38.33. Ignoring the FPGA's NRE gives 6,800 units.

clk toggles every 5 ns, so the period is 10 ns and rising edges occur at 5, 15, …, 195 ns: 20 edges by 200 ns. A 4-bit unsigned counter wraps modulo 16, so cnt = 20 mod 16 = 4 (GHDL reports 4 after 20 edges). 20 ignores the wrap, and 8 treats 5 ns as the clock period.

questions.questionText: For normalised IEEE 754 single-precision numbers, which values can the stored 8-bit exponent field take, and which true exponents do they represent?
questions.explanation: Stored exponent 0 (zero and denormals) and 255 (infinity and NaN) are reserved, which leaves 1 to 254. Subtracting the bias 127 gives true exponents −126 to +127, so normalised magnitudes run from 2^−126 to just under 2^128.

questions.questionText: A cache designer must choose one policy for write hits and one for write misses. Which combination is the conventional pairing, for the stated reason?
options: Write-back with no-write-allocate, because a write-back cache must never fetch a block on a write
Write-through with write-allocate, because write-through needs the block in the cache before memory can be updated
Write-back with write-allocate, because once the block has been fetched, later writes to it hit in the cache and cost no memory traffic
Write-through with a dirty bit on every line, so that main memory is written only when a line is evicted
questions.explanation: Write-back gains only when repeated writes hit in the cache, so it normally allocates the block on a write miss; write-through sends every write to memory anyway and is usually paired with no-write-allocate. A dirty bit belongs to write-back, not to write-through.

questions.questionText: A 5-stage pipeline with full forwarding has an ideal CPI of 1 and runs at 1.3 GHz. 25% of the instructions are loads, and 40% of the loads are immediately followed by an instruction that uses the loaded value (1 stall cycle each). 20% of the instructions are branches; the pipeline predicts not-taken, half of the branches are taken, and each taken branch costs 2 cycles. There are no other stalls. What are the effective CPI and the MIPS rating?
questions.explanation: CPI = 1 + 0.25 × 0.4 × 1 + 0.2 × 0.5 × 2 = 1 + 0.1 + 0.2 = 1.3, and MIPS = f / (CPI × 10^6) = 1300 / 1.3 = 1000. Charging every branch gives CPI 1.5, stalling after every load gives 1.45, and 1690 comes from multiplying by the CPI instead of dividing.

questions.questionText: A negative-feedback amplifier has forward gain G = 500 and feedback gain H = 0.1. Its closed-loop gain is often approximated by 1/H. What is the exact closed-loop gain, and by what percentage does 1/H overstate it?
questions.explanation: Exact gain = G / (1 + GH) = 500 / 51 ≈ 9.80. 1/H = 10, and (10 − 9.80) / 9.80 = 1/(GH) = 1/50 = 2%, so the approximation improves as the loop gain GH grows. 454.5 comes from wrongly using G / (1 + H).

questions.questionText: Which pairing of addressing mode and effective address (EA) is NOT correct?
options: Indexed: EA = index register + address field
Indirect: EA = the address field itself
Register indirect: EA = contents of the named register
questions.explanation: In indirect addressing the address field points to a memory word that holds the EA, so EA = M[address field]; EA = address field is direct addressing. The other three pairings are the standard definitions.

questions.questionText: 32 processors are to be interconnected. Which set of figures is correct for a 32 × 32 crossbar, a 32 × 32 omega network built from 2 × 2 switches, and a 5-dimensional hypercube?
options: Crossbar 1024 crosspoints; omega 160 switches in 5 stages; hypercube diameter 5
Crossbar 1024 crosspoints; omega 80 switches in 5 stages; hypercube diameter 16
Crossbar 64 crosspoints; omega 80 switches in 5 stages; hypercube diameter 5
Crossbar 1024 crosspoints; omega 80 switches in 5 stages; hypercube diameter 5
questions.explanation: Crossbar: 32 × 32 = 1024 crosspoints. Omega: log₂32 = 5 stages of 32/2 = 16 switches, i.e. 80 switches. Hypercube: 2^5 = 32 nodes with 5 links each, and the farthest nodes differ in all 5 address bits, so the diameter is 5.

questions.questionText: A system's main memory takes 80 ns per access. A cache with a 4 ns access time is added; main memory is started only after a cache miss has been detected, so a miss costs 4 + 80 ns, and 95% of accesses hit. What is the new average access time, and by what factor does the cache speed up memory accesses?
questions.explanation: t = 0.95 × 4 + 0.05 × (4 + 80) = 3.8 + 4.2 = 8.0 ns (the same as 4 + 0.05 × 80). Without the cache every access takes 80 ns, so the speedup is 80 / 8 = 10. 7.8 ns is the simultaneous-access formula, and 20 is only t_m / t_c.

questions.questionText: A 16-bit multiplier holds 0000 0000 1111 1111 (255). How many add or subtract operations does Booth's algorithm perform, and how many additions does the plain shift-and-add method perform?
questions.explanation: Booth acts only where adjacent multiplier bits differ: a subtraction at bit 0 (pair Q0 Q−1 = 10) and an addition at bit 8 (pair 01), because 255 = 2^8 − 2^0. Shift-and-add adds the multiplicand once for every 1 bit, i.e. 8 times.

questions.questionText: Which pairing of RTOS object and typical use is NOT correct?
options: Mutex — mutual exclusion with an owner, usually with priority inheritance
Counting semaphore initialised to N — guarding a pool of N identical resources
Mailbox — an unbounded stream of bytes without message boundaries
Event group (event flags) — waiting until a combination of events has occurred
questions.explanation: A byte stream without message boundaries is a pipe; a mailbox passes discrete messages (in µC/OS-II, one pointer-sized message at a time), so message boundaries are kept. The mutex, counting-semaphore and event-group pairings are the standard ones.

questions.questionText: Mano's basic computer has 25 instructions. How many of them are memory-reference, register-reference and input-output instructions, respectively?
questions.explanation: Opcodes 000–110 give 7 memory-reference instructions (AND, ADD, LDA, STA, BUN, BSA, ISZ). Opcode 111 with I = 0 gives 12 register-reference instructions, one per bit of IR(0–11), and with I = 1 it gives 6 I/O instructions (INP, OUT, SKI, SKO, ION, IOF): 7 + 12 + 6 = 25.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. u is unsigned(7 downto 0) holding "10010110". What are rotate_left(u, 3) and shift_left(u, 3)?
questions.explanation: rotate_left moves the three leftmost bits 100 round to the right end: 10110 & 100 = "10110100". shift_left discards them and fills with zeros: "10110000" (both confirmed in GHDL). "11010010" and "00010010" are the rotate_right and shift_right results.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit system with a 16-bit address bus (byte-addressable) needs 32 KB of RAM starting at 8000H, built from 8K × 4 chips (K = 1024). How many chips are needed, and which address range does the last row of chips occupy?
questions.explanation: (32K / 8K) × (8 / 4) = 4 rows of 2 chips = 8 chips. Each row holds 8 KB = 2000H bytes, so the rows occupy 8000H–9FFFH, A000H–BFFFH, C000H–DFFFH and E000H–FFFFH (A12–A0 go to every chip, and A14–A13 drive a 2-to-4 decoder enabled when A15 = 1). 4 chips forgets that two 4-bit chips make one byte.

questions.questionText: A UART receives a continuous stream at 115,200 baud in 8N1 format (1 start bit, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit) and raises one interrupt per received character. Each interrupt costs the CPU 20 µs in total. What fraction of CPU time do these interrupts take?
questions.explanation: Each character occupies 10 bit times, so 115,200 / 10 = 11,520 characters/s, and the load is 11,520 × 20 µs = 0.2304 ≈ 23.0%. Counting only the 8 data bits gives 28.8%, and 11-bit frames (with a parity bit) would give 20.9%.

questions.questionText: Which pairing of pipeline hazard and remedy is NOT correct?
options: Data (RAW) hazard — forwarding the result from a pipeline register to the ALU input
Control hazard — branch prediction or a delayed branch
Structural hazard — separate instruction and data memories (split caches)
questions.explanation: A control hazard arises because the next PC is unknown until a branch resolves, which prediction, delayed branches or early resolution address. Register renaming removes WAR and WAW name dependences, which are data hazards. Duplicating a resource cures a structural hazard, and forwarding cures most RAW hazards.

questions.questionText: The IEEE 754 single-precision words 4120 0000H and 3FC0 0000H are added. What is the result, as a single-precision word?
questions.explanation: 4120 0000H = 1.25 × 2^3 = 10.0 and 3FC0 0000H = 1.5 × 2^0 = 1.5. Aligning 1.5 to exponent 3 gives 0.1875 × 2^3, and 1.25 + 0.1875 = 1.4375 = 1.0111b, so the sum is 1.0111b × 2^3 = 11.5: sign 0, exponent 130 = 1000 0010, fraction 0111 0…0, i.e. 4138 0000H. 40B8 0000H and 41B8 0000H have the exponent off by one.

questions.questionText: Jobs J1, J2 and J3 arrive at time 0 in that order with CPU bursts of 8, 2 and 4 ms. What is the average turnaround time under FCFS and under non-pre-emptive SJF, respectively?
questions.explanation: FCFS completes the jobs at 8, 10 and 14 ms: (8 + 10 + 14) / 3 = 10.67 ms. SJF runs J2, J3 and then J1, finishing at 2, 6 and 14 ms: 22 / 3 = 7.33 ms. 6.00 and 2.67 ms are the average waiting times, and 14 ms is only the finishing time of the last job.

questions.questionText: Which pairing of IC technology and the part of the chip that is made specially for a design is NOT correct?
options: Full-custom — every mask layer, with transistors and wiring laid out for the design
Standard cell — every mask layer, but built from pre-designed library cells
FPGA — only the metal interconnect layers, which the foundry adds after the chip is bought
Gate array — only the metal interconnect layers over prefabricated transistors
questions.explanation: An FPGA is completely fabricated before purchase and no masks are made for the design; it is configured in the field by loading programming bits. Custom metal layers over a prefabricated transistor array describe a masked gate array.

questions.questionText: A word-addressable memory holds 256K words of 32 bits (K = 1024). How wide must the memory address register (MAR) and the memory buffer (data) register (MBR) be?
questions.explanation: 256K = 2^18 words need an 18-bit address, and each access transfers one 32-bit word, so MBR is 32 bits. 20 address bits would be needed only if the same 1 MB were byte-addressable.

questions.questionText: A cache has 64 lines, and main-memory block number 1000 is loaded into it. Which line does the block occupy if the cache is direct-mapped, and which set if the same cache is organised as 4-way set-associative?
questions.explanation: Direct mapping: line = 1000 mod 64 = 40. 4-way: 64 / 4 = 16 sets, so set = 1000 mod 16 = 8. Set 0 comes from 1000 mod 4 (the number of ways instead of sets), and 15 and 62 are the quotients 1000 div 64 and 1000 div 16, which form the tags.

questions.questionText: Which pairing of a MESI state with its meaning is correct?
options: Exclusive — this is the only cached copy, and it still matches main memory
Shared — the line has been written, so main memory is out of date
Modified — the line may also be valid in other caches
Invalid — the line holds valid data that must be written back first
questions.explanation: Exclusive means clean and held by this cache alone, so a write can move it to Modified without a bus transaction. Shared is clean and possibly in other caches, Modified is dirty and held only here, and Invalid holds no valid data.

questions.questionText: Mano's microprogrammed computer uses a 128 × 20 control memory (F1, F2, F3 of 3 bits each, CD 2, BR 2 and AD 7 bits). If the control memory is enlarged to 256 words while the micro-operation fields stay the same, what are the new microinstruction width and the total control-memory size?
questions.explanation: Only the address field grows: 256 words need an 8-bit AD, so each word becomes 9 + 2 + 2 + 8 = 21 bits and the memory holds 256 × 21 = 5376 bits. The F fields depend on the number of micro-operations, not on the number of words.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the three terms of a PID controller is NOT correct?
options: The proportional term acts on the present error, and too large a gain causes oscillation
The integral term accumulates past error and removes steady-state error
The derivative term removes steady-state error, so a PD controller never leaves one
The derivative term acts on the rate of change of the error, adding damping but amplifying noise
questions.explanation: A constant error has zero derivative, so the D term cannot remove a steady-state error; that is the job of the integral term. The other three statements are the standard effects of P, I and D.

questions.questionText: A device delivers 100,000 bytes per second. With interrupt-driven I/O each byte costs the CPU 5 µs of interrupt overhead. With DMA the data moves in 1000-byte blocks, and each block costs the CPU 20 µs for set-up and the completion interrupt. What fraction of CPU time does each method use?
questions.explanation: Interrupts: 100,000 × 5 µs = 0.5 s per second = 50%. DMA: 100,000 / 1000 = 100 blocks/s × 20 µs = 2 ms per second = 0.2%. DMA pays the software overhead once per block instead of once per byte.

questions.questionText: In IEEE 754 single precision, what is the gap between consecutive representable numbers in the interval [1, 2), and in the interval [1024, 2048)?
questions.explanation: With 23 fraction bits, one unit in the last place is 2^−23 × 2^e. In [1, 2) e = 0, giving 2^−23 ≈ 1.19 × 10^−7; in [1024, 2048) e = 10, giving 2^−13 ≈ 1.22 × 10^−4. The absolute gap grows with the exponent while the relative precision stays near 7 decimal digits.

questions.questionText: A microcontroller's watchdog timer counts a 32.768 kHz clock divided by a prescaler of 64, and it resets the system when its count reaches 4096. What is the longest interval the software may leave between two watchdog refreshes?
questions.explanation: The watchdog tick is 64 / 32,768 Hz ≈ 1.95 ms, so the count of 4096 is reached after 4096 × 64 / 32,768 = 8 s, and the software must refresh the watchdog within 8 s. Forgetting the prescaler gives 0.125 s, and 1.95 ms is only one prescaled tick.

questions.questionText: Which pair of features belongs to the classic CISC design style?
options: Load/store architecture and a large general-purpose register file
Overlapped register windows and delayed branches
questions.explanation: CISC machines such as the VAX and x86 use variable-length instructions with many formats and addressing modes, traditionally decoded by microprogrammed control. The other three pairs are RISC features (MIPS, SPARC, ARM, RISC-V).

questions.questionText: A 5-dimensional hypercube multicomputer uses store-and-forward routing over links of 100 MB/s (1 MB = 10^6 bytes). Ignoring start-up and header delays, what is the worst-case time to deliver a 1000-byte message between two nodes?
questions.explanation: The farthest nodes are 5 hops apart (the diameter of a 5-cube), and each hop must receive the whole message: 1000 B / 100 MB/s = 10 µs, so 5 × 10 µs = 50 µs. 10 µs is a single hop, 160 µs assumes N/2 = 16 hops, and 400 µs treats the link rate as 100 Mbit/s.

questions.questionText: Which list gives the Liu and Layland rate-monotonic utilisation bound n(2^(1/n) − 1) for n = 1, n = 2 and n → ∞?
questions.explanation: n = 1: 1 × (2 − 1) = 1; n = 2: 2(√2 − 1) ≈ 0.828; as n grows the bound falls towards ln 2 ≈ 0.693. 0.780 is the value for n = 3.

questions.questionText: A 4-way set-associative cache holds 32 KB of data in 64-byte lines for a processor with 32-bit byte addresses (1 KB = 1024 bytes). Its hit time is 2 ns, its miss rate is 4% and its miss penalty is 50 ns. Using AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty, what are the tag width and the average memory access time?
questions.explanation: 32 KB / 64 B = 512 lines and 512 / 4 = 128 sets, so the set field is 7 bits, the offset 6 bits and the tag 32 − 7 − 6 = 19 bits. AMAT = 2 + 0.04 × 50 = 4.0 ns. 17 bits is the direct-mapped tag (9 line bits), and 26 bits the fully associative one.

questions.questionText: Which pairing of formula and quantity is NOT correct?
options: S = nk / (k + n − 1) — speedup of a k-stage pipeline over n tasks
U = Σ C_i/T_i ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1) — sufficient schedulability test for rate-monotonic scheduling
Y/R = G / (1 − GH) — closed-loop gain of a negative-feedback system
t = h·t_c + (1 − h)·t_m — average access time when cache and memory are accessed simultaneously
questions.explanation: Negative feedback gives Y/R = G / (1 + GH); G / (1 − GH) is the positive-feedback case. The pipeline, RM-bound and simultaneous-access formulas are paired correctly.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008. Given type color_t is (RED, GREEN, BLUE, WHITE, BLACK);, what are color_t'succ(GREEN), color_t'val(3) and color_t'pos(color_t'high)?
questions.explanation: Positions count from 0: RED 0, GREEN 1, BLUE 2, WHITE 3, BLACK 4. So 'succ(GREEN) is BLUE, 'val(3) is WHITE, and 'high is BLACK at position 4 (GHDL reports blue, white and 4). Counting from 1 gives the answers with 5, and RED is 'pred(GREEN).

questions.questionText: A serial flash chip holds 64 Mibit (1 Mibit = 2^20 bits) and is erased in 4 KiB sectors (1 KiB = 1024 bytes). How many bytes does it hold, and how many sectors does it have?
questions.explanation: 64 × 2^20 bits / 8 = 2^23 = 8,388,608 bytes, and 2^23 / 2^12 = 2048 sectors of 4 KiB. Decimal prefixes give 8,000,000 bytes, treating bits as bytes gives 67,108,864 bytes, and 16,384 would be 512-byte sectors.

questions.questionText: A byte-addressable RISC has 32-bit instructions. A conditional branch holds a 6-bit opcode, two 5-bit register fields and a two's-complement word offset in all the remaining bits, with target = (PC + 4) + 4 × offset. What range of byte distances from PC + 4 can the branch reach?
questions.explanation: The offset has 32 − 6 − 5 − 5 = 16 bits, i.e. −32,768 to +32,767 words; multiplying by 4 gives −131,072 to +131,068 bytes. Forgetting the × 4 gives the first option, reading the offset as unsigned gives the third, and counting only one register field (a 21-bit offset) gives ±4 M.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly compares the three DMA transfer modes?
options: Transparent DMA is the fastest mode, because it never has to wait for the CPU
Cycle stealing moves a block faster than burst mode, because it interleaves with the CPU
Burst mode gives the highest transfer rate but keeps the CPU off the bus longest; transparent DMA never slows the CPU but is the slowest; cycle stealing lies between
All three modes move a block equally fast; they differ only in when the CPU is interrupted
questions.explanation: Burst mode holds the bus for the whole block, cycle stealing takes one bus cycle at a time and delays the CPU slightly per word, and transparent DMA uses only cycles the CPU leaves idle, so it costs the CPU nothing but has the lowest and least predictable rate.

questions.questionText: A number whose true (unbiased) exponent is +5 is stored in IEEE 754 single precision and in double precision. What are the stored exponent fields, in decimal?
questions.explanation: Stored exponent = true exponent + bias: 5 + 127 = 132 in the 8-bit field and 5 + 1023 = 1028 in the 11-bit field. Subtracting the bias gives 122 and 1018, and 133 and 1029 use biases of 128 and 1024.
